newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge fines Bayer AG unit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge fines Bayer AG unit.

text.p: A U.S. District Judge on Wednesday fined Bayer AG's U.S. subsidiary $50 million for taking part in an international conspiracy to fix prices and allocate sales for citric acid.

Judge Fern Smith accepted a plea agreement reached between the U.S. Justice Department and Haarmann & Reimer Corp, the Springfield, New Jersey-based subsidiary of the German pharmaceutical and chemical giant.
The agreement was announced earlier Wednesday by the Justice Department.
Smith also sentenced Hans Hartmann, a senior executive at Haarmann & Reimer's German counterpart, to a fine of $150,000, also in line with the plea agreement.

At a hearing in federal court in San Francisco, Haarmann & Reimer Corp and Hartmann, a German citizen, pleaded guilty to taking part in an international conspiracy to fix citric acid prices. Richard White, Haarmann & Reimer Corp's chairman, entered the guilty plea on the company's behalf.

Smith set a five-year schedule for Haarmann & Reimer to pay the $50 million fine. The first $10 million must be paid within 30 days and the remaining $40 million in five annual installments of $8 million each starting on the first anniversary of sentencing.
Smith noted that she had the power to order restitution to the victims of the price fixing. But she said she saw no further need for restitution because of a pending civil case.
Under the agreement, Hartmann, 62, was not sentenced to any jail or probation time and would still be able to travel to the United States.
Justice Department attorneys said at the hearing that Haarmann & Reimer Corp sold $400 million of citric acid in the United States during the period of the alleged conspiracy.
The Justice Department's attorneys said Haarmann & Reimer could have been liable to a much heavier fine under sentencing guidelines.

But they said they believed the $50 million fine was appropriate because of the substantial cooperation the company had provided to the government and the significant role it had played in seeking the cooperation of other co-conspirators.
They also agreed on a lesser sentence for Hartmann than he could have faced because he also cooperated.
Smith accepted the plea agreement and the sentencing agreement, saying: "I think the reasoning set forth by the United States is valid."
